analysis.one_liner: Requires federal pathogen-reduction performance standards and enforcement for meat and poultry processing plants.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: it sat in the Senate Agriculture Committee for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Agriculture Department to survey how contaminated raw meat and poultry actually are, set public health goals for cutting foodborne illness, and write enforceable pathogen-reduction performance standards that processing plants must meet — standards calibrated to what the best-performing plants already achieve. Plants that repeatedly failed and did not correct the problem could lose the right to label their products "inspected and passed." It would also have created a scientific advisory committee and required enforcement of existing sanitation and HACCP food-safety rules. The bill never left the Senate Agriculture Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry — essentially everyone who buys food — gain a food supply with lower levels of dangerous pathogens like E. coli and Salmonella, because processing plants would face enforceable contamination standards based on what the cleanest plants already achieve, backed by the threat of losing the "inspected and passed" label. Federal food safety enforcement also gains clearer legal authority and independent scientific advice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who buys meat and poultry

how_it_helps.text: The bill required the Agriculture Secretary to conduct statistically representative surveys of how much foodborne-pathogen contamination exists in raw meat and poultry, publish the results, and repeat the surveys at least every three years — giving the public and regulators real data on contamination levels, including variation from plant to plant.

It required the Secretary to write enforceable pathogen-reduction performance standards for meat and poultry, set to the lowest contamination level reasonably achievable and calibrated against what the best-performing quartile of plants already achieve — meaning the standards push laggard plants to meet a bar the industry has already shown it can reach.

It gave the Secretary a concrete enforcement tool: a plant that repeatedly fails a pathogen standard or the sanitation and HACCP requirements and does not correct the problem could be barred from labeling its products as 'inspected and passed,' which would make the product unsellable in commerce.

It directed the Secretary to set measurable public health goals for reducing foodborne illness, updated every two years using CDC data, and to report to Congress on the feasibility of health-based standards — building a framework for judging whether food safety rules actually make people less sick.

It established a National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods to give independent scientific advice on food safety standards, with conflict-of-interest rules barring members with conflicts from voting.

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processing plants would bear the cost of meeting pathogen-reduction standards: testing, process changes, and potential loss of the "inspected and passed" label if they failed repeatedly without correcting the problem. Some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers in the form of slightly higher meat and poultry prices.

drawbacks.text: The standards would impose real compliance costs on meat and poultry processors — new testing, process changes, and possible loss of the 'inspected and passed' label for failing plants — costs that could be passed on to consumers in the price of meat and poultry.

Calibrating standards to what 'upper quartile' plants already achieve is aggressive: it assumes best-in-class performance can be generalized to every establishment, including small processors with less capital and technical capacity, and industry could have challenged the standards in court under the bill's own terms (which only bar challenges claiming the Secretary lacks authority).

The bill layers a new advisory committee, surveys, annual reports, and rulemaking deadlines on top of existing HACCP requirements, adding administrative machinery that critics could call duplicative of USDA's existing authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is real: foodborne illness from meat and poultry pathogens is a significant disease burden, and the bill's approach — survey actual contamination, set goals, write standards based on what the best plants already achieve — was the design a 2003 National Academy of Sciences report had recommended, which gives it strong technical grounding. The cost is borne by processing plants, especially the laggards, and some of it would likely reach consumers as slightly higher meat prices; it could also have triggered litigation over the standards. On balance this was a moderate, well-grounded public health measure whose main weakness may have been that it addressed a diffuse, invisible risk (pathogen contamination) rather than a visible one, giving the public little way to demand a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill on June 30, 2005 with seven cosponsors, including one Republican (Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania).
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day — the only action it ever received.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a vote, reported the bill out, or scheduled floor time, and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors are better off: they face no enforceable pathogen-reduction performance standards and keep the current inspection system, in which plants can label products 'inspected and passed' without meeting pathogen limits. Consumers continue to bear the risk of pathogen contamination that the bill would have reduced.

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 30, 2005, with introductory remarks, to write enforceable pathogen-reduction standards into federal meat and poultry inspection law.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Republican among the original eight supporters.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 30, 2005 and took no further action on it — no hearings, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 18 months of the 109th Congress.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory pathogen-reduction performance standards and tougher HACCP enforcement, arguing existing inspection sufficed and new standards would impose costs.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction — one Republican (Specter) among eight original cosponsors — but no vote ever occurred, so the partisan shape of any floor fight is unknown; the record shows no recorded opposition at all.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed mandatory pathogen-reduction performance standards, regular microbial testing, and enforceable sanitation rules on processing plants, with the loss of the 'inspected and passed' label for non-compliant plants. Compliance would cost plants money, but the bill explicitly calibrated standards to what top-quartile plants already achieve, meaning leaders would face little burden.

industries.industry: Federal meat and poultry inspection status quo
industries.note: The current inspection system has continued to run without pathogen performance standards, so the industry's existing regulatory arrangement — in which 'inspected and passed' labeling does not guarantee pathogen limits — was locked in for another Congress. That is the practical effect of the bill dying in committee rather than a provision of the bill itself.
